summary: Comments on the File Transfer Protocol. It is an old version of the discussion and was replaced by RFC 624, with related views in RFCs 614, 542 and 640.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 607 lists proposed small changes to make early FTP servers and clients easier to implement. It focuses on commands, replies, and data-transfer details, and was later obsoleted by RFC 624 and updated by RFC 614.

subtitle: A 1974 memo proposing small changes to simplify early FTP implementations.

tldr.problem: The authors found that FTP's command and reply rules forced client programs to handle many special cases.
tldr.mechanism: The memo lists thirteen proposed fixes, including regular command lengths, clearer reply codes, fixed reply ordering, and bounded line lengths.
tldr.outcome: RFC 607 was obsoleted by RFC 624 and updated by RFC 614.

today: RFC 607 was obsoleted by RFC 624 and updated by RFC 614.

sections.title: Small Fixes for FTP
sections.content:
The authors distinguish basic problems that would require substantial design changes from issues that could be addressed with little effort. This memo covers the latter and gives a proposed solution for each listed problem.

Many proposals aim to reduce special cases in an FTP client, especially when it decides whether a command succeeded or how to parse a reply.
sections.plainLanguage: The memo is a list of relatively small changes its authors thought would make FTP easier to build. It does not attempt to redesign the whole protocol.

sections.title: Commands and Transfer Ordering
sections.content:
The proposals include adding an ACTV command to switch a server from passive back to active mode and using four-letter command verbs, replacing the three-letter BYE. They also propose sending a 250 reply before attempting to open a data connection, so the client knows which event to wait for first.

The memo proposes that a server return success when it skips an unneeded command. For blocked-mode transfers, it says data after the final end-of-record marker and before end of file should be discarded.
sections.plainLanguage: Make command names more regular and tell the client what is happening in a predictable order. That gives client programs fewer special cases to handle.

sections.title: Making Replies Easier to Parse
sections.content:
The memo proposes one distinct first digit for successful replies and another for replies meant only for human readers. It also suggests a unique code such as 009 for continuation lines in a multi-line reply and a maximum nesting depth for such replies.

Other proposals ask for specified maximum lengths for TELNET lines and several FTP arguments. The final item points out that reply code 331 may be a typographical error in cases where the memo believes 332 LOGIN FIRST, PLEASE is intended.
sections.plainLanguage: The authors want programs to recognize success and continuation replies using simple, consistent rules. They also want limits that let programs know how much input space to reserve.
